title: Week 41
body: late term. monitoring is routine now, and induction is usually the next conversation. the baby is still growing and still moving. the placenta is aging, which is why monitoring matters now. the baby is ready to be born. you may have strong braxton hicks, more pelvic pressure, and trouble sleeping. your cervix may be dilated. you may feel more tired than at any point in the pregnancy. being past 41 weeks is tiring in a way that is hard to explain. it is not a failure and it is not unusual. ask for the monitoring schedule so the days have a shape.

title: Go to the monitoring appointments
body: past 41 weeks the placenta can age, and monitoring is how they check the baby is still doing well. skipping one is the one thing not to do this week. expect a non-stress test, which watches the heart rate for about twenty minutes, and possibly an ultrasound. these are quick and they are the reason it is safe to wait. if a test looks off, they will talk about induction that day. you are already being monitored on a schedule. non-stress test biophysical profile

title: Decide about induction
body: most practices recommend induction by 42 weeks. deciding now means you are choosing, not being told. ask what date they recommend and what the alternatives are. waiting with monitoring is an option at many practices. ask how long an induction usually takes, what the methods are, and whether you can eat and move during it. write the answers down. you already have a date or a plan. book the induction wait with monitoring

title: Ask whether a membrane sweep is worth trying
body: it is a low-risk option that can start labor without medication. it does not always work, and it is worth knowing the trade-off. a sweep is done during an exam and separates the membranes from the cervix. it can cause cramping and spotting and it can start labor within a couple of days. it is not recommended if your water has broken or you are group b strep positive without antibiotics in place. ask your ob whether it fits your situation. you have already discussed it, or your water has broken. try it skip it

title: The placenta ages, and that is why monitoring exists
body: past 41 weeks the placenta works less well. monitoring catches that early. it is the reason the extra appointments are worth the trip.

title: Movement is still the signal
body: if the pattern changes, call. do not wait for the next appointment and do not use a doppler to decide.

title: The waiting is genuinely hard
body: being past 41 weeks is exhausting in a way that is hard to explain to people who are not there. tell someone. ask your ob for the schedule so the days have a shape.

title: Week 42
body: the last week of the range. induction is usually the plan now. the baby is post-term. the skin may be a little dry and the nails long. the baby is ready to be born, and the placenta is the reason not to wait much longer. you may be very tired, very uncomfortable, and very ready. your cervix may be dilated. contractions may be stronger and more frequent. this is the hardest week for most people. it is not a reflection of anything you did. ask for help with the waiting, and let people bring food.

title: Go in for the induction
body: past 42 weeks the risks of waiting go up for both of you. induction is the recommended path, and it is a plan rather than an emergency. bring the bag, the id, the insurance card, and the car seat. eat before you go if they let you. expect it to take a day or more — inductions are slow, especially with a first baby. ask what the first step is so you know what is happening. you are already in labor or already induced. a scheduled induction go in today

title: Keep every monitoring appointment
body: if you are waiting rather than inducing, monitoring is what makes waiting safe. it is the whole reason the wait is allowed. expect a non-stress test and possibly an ultrasound, twice a week at many practices. if a test looks off, they will talk about induction that day. do not skip one because you are tired — that is exactly the week not to skip. you are already induced or in labor. non-stress test biophysical profile

title: Tell someone how you are doing
body: the last week is isolating. saying it out loud to one person makes it smaller, and it is the week people most often go quiet. tell your partner, a friend, or your ob. if you are feeling hopeless or thinking about hurting yourself, call or text 988. that is not an overreaction — it is the right number for that feeling. you are doing well and have people around you. tell one person call or text 988

title: Post-term is a medical word, not a judgement
body: it means past 42 weeks. it is common enough that practices have a routine for it. it is not something you caused.

title: Inductions are slow
body: a first induction often takes a day or more. bring something to do, snacks if allowed, and a support person who can stay. it is not an emergency — it is a process.

title: Movement is still the signal
body: if the pattern changes, call. do not wait for the next appointment and do not use a doppler to decide.

title: The first week
body: you are not supposed to feel like yourself yet. nobody does in the first week. your baby is learning to eat, sleep, and regulate their temperature, and is not good at any of it yet. they will lose up to 10% of their birth weight and regain it by about two weeks. that is expected. bleeding like a heavy period, afterpains when you feed, and stitches or a incision that need looking after. your milk may come in around day three, often with engorgement and a lot of leaking. the 'baby blues' affect up to 80% of people in the first two weeks — tearfulness, irritability, feeling overwhelmed. it usually lifts by day ten. if it does not, or if it gets worse, that is postpartum depression and it is treatable.

title: Feed the baby eight to twelve times a day
body: frequent feeding in the first week is what builds your supply and what clears the bilirubin that causes jaundice. eight to twelve feeds in 24 hours, including at night. wake the baby if they sleep longer than three hours in the first two weeks. if breastfeeding hurts beyond the first few seconds of latch, that is a sign to get help, not to push through. a lactation consultant is covered by most insurance under the aca, often with no copay. your pediatrician has given you a different feeding plan for a medical reason. a lactation consultant through insurance la leche league formula

title: Go to the 3-to-5-day visit
body: this visit checks the weight loss, the jaundice, and the feeding. it is the most important appointment of the first month. bring your discharge papers and any questions. they will weigh the baby, check the cord or circumcision, and watch a feed if you ask. ask them to show you how to tell if the baby is getting enough — wet diapers and swallowing sounds, not just time at the breast. your pediatrician has already seen the baby and set a different schedule. your pediatrician's office

title: Take the postpartum screening seriously
body: you will be asked about your mood at your postpartum visit. answer honestly, because postpartum depression and anxiety are common and treatable, and nobody is judging you. about 1 in 8 people get postpartum depression. symptoms include not sleeping even when the baby sleeps, feeling numb rather than sad, intrusive frightening thoughts, and feeling like your family would be better off without you. any of those is a reason to call, not to wait. the national maternal mental health hotline is free, 24/7, and you do not need a diagnosis to call. you are feeling well, and you know the numbers if that changes. psi helpline national maternal mental health hotline 988

title: Jaundice
body: most newborns get some yellowing around day three to five. it is usually harmless and clears. call your pediatrician if the yellow spreads to the belly or legs, if the baby is very sleepy, or if feeding drops off.

title: Visitors
body: you are allowed to say no. a useful rule: visitors bring food or do a chore, and they do not stay longer than an hour.

title: Sleep when the baby sleeps is bad advice
body: it is well meant and often impossible. what actually helps is one protected four-hour stretch where someone else handles the baby. ask for that instead.

title: Pain relief
body: ibuprofen and acetaminophen are compatible with breastfeeding. take them on schedule rather than waiting for the pain to peak.

title: The second week
body: the visitors have gone home and the nights are long. this is the week it usually gets harder before it gets easier. your baby is back to birth weight or close to it, and is awake for longer stretches. they can see about a foot away, which is exactly the distance to your face while feeding. bleeding is lighter and browner. afterpains are milder. if you had a tear or a caesarean, the wound is knitting but still sore, and you may still be taking stool softeners. the baby blues usually lift by day ten. if the tearfulness is getting worse instead of better, that is worth saying out loud to your ob or midwife at the next visit.

title: Weigh the baby at the two-week visit
body: birth weight is usually back by now. if it is not, the visit is where you find out why, and the fix is usually a feeding change rather than anything serious. the two-week visit is the last of the early weight checks. bring the discharge papers and write down how many feeds and wet diapers you had yesterday, because that is what they will ask.

title: Feed on cue, not on a schedule
body: a two-week-old who is fed whenever they show hunger cues is easier to feed and easier to settle than one held to a clock. early cues are stirring, rooting, and hands to the mouth. crying is a late cue, and a crying baby is harder to latch. expect eight to twelve feeds in 24 hours, and expect cluster feeding in the evening.

title: Take a sleep shift, not a sleep night
body: four hours of broken sleep is not the same as four hours in a row. one protected stretch is what makes the rest survivable. pick a four-hour window and hand the baby to someone else for all of it, with a bottle if you are not feeding. earplugs and a closed door are part of the plan, not a luxury.

title: Jaundice usually peaks and fades
body: jaundice is common in the first week and usually fades by two weeks. it is the reason for the weight check. call the pediatrician the same day if the yellow spreads to the palms or soles, or if the baby is hard to wake for feeds.

title: You can say no to visitors
body: a short visit is not a small thing when you are feeding every two hours. it is fine to say the baby is not ready for visitors yet, and it is fine to ask people to come back next month.

title: The third week
body: milk is in, the bleeding is easing, and the baby has opinions now. your baby is starting to track a face and may hold eye contact for a few seconds. they are stronger at the breast or bottle and can take more at a feed, which is why the feeds start to space out a little. engorgement is settling. if you are breastfeeding, you may feel let-down as a tingle or a sharp ache. your abdomen is shrinking back, and the linea nigra is still there and will fade slowly. this is the week the adrenaline runs out. if you are crying more than last week rather than less, tell someone at the next visit.

title: Know what a good feed looks like
body: supply is set by how often milk leaves, not by how much you can pump. watching the baby rather than the pump is the more accurate signal. a good feed has rhythmic sucking with audible swallows, and the baby comes off relaxed with milk at the corner of the mouth. six or more wet diapers a day and pale urine are the other signs. pumped volume is not a measure of supply.

title: Start tummy time, a minute at a time
body: tummy time builds the neck and shoulder strength that comes before rolling, sitting, and crawling. two or three short sessions a day is enough at this age. do it while the baby is awake and not hungry, on a firm surface, with you right there. a baby who hates it will tolerate it longer on your chest.

title: Answer the mood questions honestly at the next visit
body: postpartum depression is common, treatable, and easy to miss when everyone is asking about the baby instead of you. the screening is a short set of questions about the last seven days. answer them as you actually are, not as you hope to be. treatment works, and it does not mean anyone takes the baby away.

title: Growth spurts are real and temporary
body: around three weeks, six weeks, and three months, a baby feeds far more for two or three days and then settles. it is not a sign your supply is failing. feed more and it passes.

title: Baby acne is not a rash to treat
body: small red bumps on the cheeks and forehead are common from two to four weeks and clear on their own. wash with water only. do not use creams or oils on it.

title: The fourth week
body: one month in. the fog is thinning, and the baby is starting to look at you on purpose. your baby can hold their head briefly when upright and is beginning to coo. they may follow a moving face across the room. hands are still fists most of the time. bleeding is usually down to spotting or gone. if you had a caesarean, the incision is closed but the area around it may still be numb. your hair may start shedding in a few weeks, which is normal and temporary. the one-month mark is when a lot of people feel worse rather than better, because the help has gone and the sleep has not come back. that is a reason to be screened, not a reason to wait.

title: Go to the one-month visit
body: this is the visit where the mood screening happens, the feeding is reviewed, and the head shape is checked. bring your questions written down, because it is easy to forget them in the room. ask about the mood screening if they do not bring it up. ask about the head shape if the baby always turns the same way.

title: Check the sleep space against the safe sleep rules
body: every sleep surface is either safe or not, and the check takes two minutes. on the back, on a firm flat surface, in the same room as you, with nothing else in the sleep space. no bumpers, no pillows, no blankets, no inclined sleepers, no car seat or swing for overnight sleep.
keywords: safe sleep back to sleep crib

title: Change the head position at every sleep
body: a baby who always lies the same way can develop a flat spot, and the fix is easier the earlier it starts. alternate which end of the crib the head goes. turn the baby's head to the other side when they are asleep and you are watching. more tummy time while awake helps too.

title: Hair loss at three months is not a sign of anything wrong
body: hair that stops shedding during pregnancy starts falling out around three to four months after birth. it is temporary and it grows back.

title: The six-week visit is yours, not the baby's
body: it is a check on your recovery: bleeding, the wound, the pelvic floor, mood, and contraception. write down what you want to ask before you go.

title: The fifth week
body: the six-week visit is next week. write your questions down now, while you remember them. your baby is cooing back at you and may smile in response to a face rather than by accident. they are awake for longer and sleep in slightly longer stretches at night. bleeding should be spotting or finished. if you are breastfeeding, your period may not return for months, and that is not a reliable sign of anything. sleep deprivation builds. if you are snapping at people or crying at small things, that is the sleep talking, and it is also worth mentioning at the visit.

title: Book the six-week postpartum visit
body: this is the visit that clears you for exercise, checks the wound and the pelvic floor, and covers contraception. ask for a pelvic floor check, not just a look at the wound. ask what exercise is safe to start and what to wait on. ask about contraception you actually want, including options that do not affect milk supply.
keywords: six week postpartum visit pelvic floor

title: Know when bleeding is not normal anymore
body: bleeding that was tapering and then gets heavier is the pattern worth calling about. spotting that comes and goes for six weeks is common. bleeding that fills a pad in an hour, passes large clots, or comes back heavy after it had stopped is not.

title: Walk outside once a day
body: daylight and gentle movement do more for mood in the first months than almost anything else you can do alone. ten minutes is enough. go at a time when someone else can hold the baby, or take the baby. it is not exercise, it is a change of scene.

title: Your period may be months away
body: if you are breastfeeding, the first period often does not return until feeds drop. that does not mean you cannot get pregnant, and it is not a contraception method.

title: A carrier buys you two hands
body: a soft structured carrier or a wrap lets you eat, walk, and answer a door. look for one that holds the baby high and tight, with the head clear and the chin off the chest.

title: The sixth week
body: the six-week visit is this week. it is the one appointment that is about you. your baby is smiling in response to you, tracking faces, and starting to make vowel sounds. they can hold their head up briefly and are stronger every day. bleeding is usually finished. the wound is healed on the outside. your core and pelvic floor are still recovering, and they will be for months. six weeks is often when the gap between what you expected and what you feel is widest. say so at the visit. it is a screening question, not a confession.

title: Go to the six-week postpartum visit
body: this is where the pelvic floor, the wound, the mood, and contraception all get looked at in one appointment. ask for an internal pelvic floor check. ask what exercise is safe now and what to wait on. ask about contraception that fits your feeding plan. ask for a referral if the mood questions are hard.

title: Start pelvic floor work, gently
body: the pelvic floor does a lot of work in pregnancy and birth, and it responds to training the same way any other muscle does. a pelvic floor physical therapist is the right person for this, and most insurance covers it. at home, the first step is learning to relax the muscles, not just squeeze them. stop if anything hurts.

title: Decide what contraception you want, and ask for it
body: fertility can return before your period does, so the decision is easier made at the visit than after. progestin-only pills, the implant, the shot, and the hormonal iud do not affect milk supply for most people. condoms and the copper iud have no hormones at all. ask what fits your plan rather than what is offered first.

title: Exercise after birth is a ramp, not a switch
body: walking first, then gentle core work, then strength. running and high-impact work usually wait until the pelvic floor has been checked. bleeding that restarts after exercise is a sign to back off.

title: The longest stretch is coming
body: between six and twelve weeks many babies start sleeping one longer stretch at night. it is not a schedule and it will change, but it is coming.

title: The seventh week
body: the visit is behind you and the baby is starting to have a rhythm. not a schedule. a rhythm. your baby is batting at toys, bringing hands to the mouth on purpose, and holding their head steadier. they may laugh out loud for the first time this month. if you are cleared for exercise, start with walking and core breathing. if you are breastfeeding, supply is usually established and engorgement is rare now. the help has gone home and the baby is more awake. this is the week a lot of people realize they have not eaten a proper meal in days.

title: Start a bedtime routine, not a bedtime
body: a short, repeated sequence is what teaches a baby that sleep is coming. the time on the clock matters less than the order. three or four steps, the same every night: feed, bath or wipe, sleep sack, dark room, a song. ten minutes is enough. do it at the same time each night and the baby starts to anticipate it.

title: Eat something with protein at every meal
body: feeding a baby burns calories, and skipping meals is what turns tired into shaky. eggs, beans, yogurt, cheese, leftover meat, peanut butter. a handful of nuts counts. if someone offers to bring food, say yes and ask for something you can eat one-handed.

title: Offer a bottle once a week if you may return to work
body: a baby who has never taken a bottle can refuse one outright at eight weeks, and that is a hard week to discover it. offer a small amount of expressed milk in a bottle at a time when the baby is calm, not starving. someone else gives it, ideally not in the room where you feed. once a week keeps the skill.
keywords: bottle pumped milk return to work

title: There is no regression at seven weeks
body: the word gets used for every change in sleep. at this age sleep is still developing, and a bad week is usually a growth spurt or a developmental leap, not a step backwards.

title: Breastfed babies need vitamin D
body: 400 iu a day from birth. formula-fed babies get it from the formula. it comes as a drop, and it is the one supplement a breastfed baby needs.

title: The eighth week
body: the two-month visit is coming, and it is the one with the first real vaccines. your baby is cooing in conversation, following you across the room, and holding their head up for longer. hands are starting to open. your hair may be shedding. your joints are still looser than usual from pregnancy hormones, which is why a return to running can feel odd. the two-month vaccines are the first decision that feels like a real one. read about them before the visit, not in the room.

title: Book the two-month visit and read the vaccine list first
body: the two-month visit is where the first set of routine vaccines happens, and knowing what is coming makes the appointment calmer. the us schedule at two months is dtap, ipv, hib, pcv, and rotavirus, and hepatitis b if it was not given at birth. ask for the vaccine information statements for each one. it is fine to ask questions and it is fine to ask them to go one at a time.

title: Tummy time, several times a day
body: tummy time is the single best thing for the strength that comes before rolling and sitting. aim for a few minutes at a time, several times a day, while the baby is awake. get down at eye level. a rolled towel under the chest helps a baby who hates it. stop when they are upset and try again later.

title: Start the childcare search if you are going back
body: good childcare in most us cities has a waitlist measured in months, and the search takes longer than people expect. ask about ratios, staff turnover, and licensing. visit in person at a time when children are awake. get on two or three waitlists rather than one. a nanny share is often cheaper than a center for one child.

title: Crying peaks around six to eight weeks
body: it is normal for crying to increase until about two months and then fall. it is not caused by anything you are doing wrong, and it is not a sign of a problem.

title: A mild fever after vaccines is common
body: fussiness, a low fever, and a sore leg for a day or two are common and expected. ask the pediatrician what dose of infant acetaminophen is right for your baby's weight before you need it.

title: The ninth week
body: the first vaccines are done. the rest of this week is about the fever rule and the crying. your baby is laughing, holding their head steady, and pushing up on their arms during tummy time. they are starting to reach for things on purpose. your supply is established if you are breastfeeding. your period may return now or much later. your core is still healing, and diastasis recti is common and treatable. the two-month mark is when a lot of people go back to work, and the week is harder than expected. plan the first week to be as small as possible.

title: Know the fever rule for a baby under three months
body: under three months, a fever is an emergency-room visit, not a wait-and-see. knowing the number now is what makes the night calmer. 100.4°f or 38°c rectally is the line. take it rectally in a baby this age, because other methods are not accurate enough. do not give fever medicine and wait to see. call the pediatrician or go in.

title: Have a plan for when the crying will not stop
body: the plan is not for the baby. it is for the moment you have been holding a screaming baby for forty minutes and you are done. put the baby down safely on their back in the crib and walk out of the room for five minutes. call someone. put in earplugs. the baby is safe in the crib and you are allowed to leave the room.

title: Check for a gap in your abdominal muscles
body: diastasis recti is common after pregnancy and it changes which exercises help and which make it worse. lie on your back with knees bent. lift your head slightly and feel along the midline above and below the belly button. a gap of two fingers or more is worth a pelvic floor physical therapist rather than a youtube program.

title: A reaction after vaccines is not a reason to skip the next one
body: a low fever, fussiness, and a sore leg are the immune system working. a serious allergic reaction is rare and looks different: swelling of the face, trouble breathing, hives. that is a 911 call.

title: The four-month sleep change is coming
body: around three to four months, sleep reorganizes into cycles closer to an adult's. it is a real developmental change, not a regression, and it passes.

title: The tenth week
body: the baby is sleeping in longer stretches and you are starting to feel like a person again. both are real. your baby is reaching for toys, bringing them to the mouth, and holding their head steady. they may be starting to roll from front to back. your hair is shedding. your joints are still loose. if you are exercising, the pelvic floor is the thing to watch, not the scale. the first three months are the hardest and they are almost over. if you are still feeling flat every day, that is worth a call rather than another month of waiting.

title: Stop swaddling once the baby shows signs of rolling
body: a swaddled baby who rolls onto their front cannot push back up, and that is the risk swaddling carries past the newborn stage. signs to watch for: rolling to one side, pushing up on the arms, or getting halfway over. when you see any of them, switch to a sleep sack with arms free. some babies roll at three months, most by five.

title: Learn the wake window for this age
body: a baby who is put down at the right level of tired settles faster than one who is overtired or not tired yet. at two to three months, most babies manage about 75 to 120 minutes awake between sleeps. watch for the first yawn and the first eye rub, and start the wind-down then. a second wind means you waited too long.

title: Check in on your mood, on purpose
body: postpartum depression can start at any point in the first year, not just the first six weeks. the screening questions are about the last seven days. if you would answer them differently than you would have a month ago, say so at the next visit. the maternal mental health line is free and answers 24 hours a day.

title: A flat spot is easier to fix now than later
body: if the back of the head is flattening on one side, more tummy time and alternating the head position at sleep usually help. ask the pediatrician at the four-month visit.

title: Drool is not teething yet
body: most babies drool heavily from two months because the salivary glands are working before the swallowing is coordinated. first teeth usually arrive between four and seven months.

title: The eleventh week
body: if you are going back to work, this is the week to practise the handover, not the week to start it. your baby is babbling with consonants, reaching accurately, and may be rolling. they recognize your face and voice from across a room. if you are pumping, supply responds to frequency and to stress. if you are not, your body is adjusting to what the baby actually takes. going back to work is a loss as well as a logistics problem. both are allowed. the first week is the worst one and it does get easier.

title: Build a small freezer stash before you go back
body: a stash is insurance, not a target. fifty ounces is plenty and two hundred is a hobby. pump once in the morning after the first feed, when supply is highest. store in two to four ounce portions so nothing is wasted. milk is good for four hours at room temperature, four days in the fridge, and six months in a freezer.

title: Do a practice handover before the first real day
body: the first day back is not the day to discover that the baby will not take a bottle from your partner. leave the baby with the caregiver for two hours while you are still nearby. write down the feed times, the nap routine, and the pediatrician's number. leave a shirt that smells like you.

title: Know your pumping rights at work
body: us law requires break time and a private space to pump for a year after birth, and the space cannot be a bathroom. the pump act covers most employees. ask for a room with a door that locks, a surface, and an outlet. ask for the breaks in writing before your first day, not on it.
keywords: pumping at work pump act breaks

title: The four-month sleep change is close
body: around three to four months, sleep cycles reorganize and night waking often increases. it is developmental, it is temporary, and it is not caused by anything you did.

title: A bottle-fed baby needs a slower flow nipple
body: a fast flow lets a baby take too much too quickly, which is why bottle-fed babies sometimes overfeed. use the slowest flow that works and pace the feed.

title: The twelfth week
body: three months. the hardest stretch is behind you, and the next stage starts next week. your baby is laughing, babbling, and may be rolling. they can see across a room and are starting to reach for what they want. bleeding is long finished. your core and pelvic floor are still healing, and they will keep healing for a year. your hair is shedding and will stop. the end of the fourth trimester is a real milestone and it is worth noticing. if you have been waiting to feel better before asking for help, this is the week to stop waiting.

title: Book the four-month visit
body: the four-month visit is the next vaccine set and the next developmental check, and the good slots go early. ask about rolling, head shape, and sleep. ask whether the baby is ready for solids yet, which is usually a conversation for the six-month visit. bring the mood screening up if it has not been asked.

title: Keep tummy time going, every day
body: tummy time is still the best thing for the strength that comes before sitting and crawling. aim for twenty to thirty minutes a day in short bursts. get down at eye level with a toy or a mirror. a baby who can push up on straight arms is getting close to rolling.

title: Decide what support you want for the next year
body: the first year is long, and the support that got you through the first three months is not the support you need for the next nine. a therapist, a parent group, a weekly call with a friend, or childcare one morning a week. pick one thing and put it in the calendar. the maternal mental health line is free if you want to talk to someone first.

title: Solids are still a few months away
body: most babies are ready around six months, when they can sit with support and hold their head steady. starting earlier does not help sleep and does not help allergies.

title: Teeth may be close
body: first teeth usually arrive between four and seven months. drool and chewing on hands start earlier and are not a sign that a tooth is imminent.

title: Month 3
body: the fourth trimester is over. the baby is a person now, and they have a schedule of their own. your baby is laughing, babbling with consonants, and holding their head steady. they can push up on their arms during tummy time and may be starting to roll. your hair is shedding and will stop in a few months. your core is still healing. if you are exercising, the pelvic floor is the thing to watch. three months is often when the adrenaline finally runs out. if you have been holding it together, this is the week it may stop working, and that is worth saying out loud.

title: Stop swaddling if the baby is rolling
body: a swaddled baby who rolls onto their front cannot push back up. that is the whole risk, and it starts the day they roll. watch for rolling to one side, pushing up on straight arms, or getting halfway over. switch to a sleep sack with the arms free. if the baby has already rolled in a swaddle, stop that night.

title: Tummy time, twenty minutes a day
body: tummy time is what builds the strength for rolling, sitting, and crawling, and it is easier to do now that the baby likes it more. short bursts add up. get down at eye level with a mirror or a toy. a rolled towel under the chest helps. stop when they are upset and try again later.

title: Know the wake window for three months
body: a baby put down at the right level of tired settles faster than one who is overtired. most three-month-olds manage about 90 to 120 minutes awake between sleeps. watch for the first yawn and the first eye rub. a second wind means you waited too long.

title: The four-month sleep change is coming
body: around three to four months, sleep reorganizes into cycles closer to an adult's. night waking often increases. it is developmental, it is temporary, and it is not caused by anything you did.

title: Drool is not teething yet
body: heavy drool from two months is the salivary glands working before the swallowing is coordinated. first teeth usually arrive between four and seven months.

title: Month 4
body: the four-month visit is this month, and the sleep change is real. both are developmental, and neither is your fault. your baby is rolling, reaching with both hands, and laughing. they can hold their head steady and are starting to bear weight on their legs when held upright. if you are breastfeeding, supply is well established. your period may have returned. your hair shedding is at its peak and will slow soon. four months is the most common time for sleep to fall apart, and the most common time for people to buy something they do not need. the change is developmental and it passes.

title: Go to the four-month visit
body: this is the second vaccine set and the developmental check where rolling and head shape get looked at. the us schedule at four months is dtap, ipv, hib, pcv, and rotavirus. ask about the head shape if the baby always turns the same way. ask what dose of infant acetaminophen is right for the baby's weight.

title: Know that the four-month sleep change is not a regression
body: sleep reorganizes into cycles closer to an adult's, which means more partial waking between cycles. it is a step forward that feels like a step back. it usually settles over two to six weeks. a consistent bedtime routine, a dark room, and a predictable wind-down help more than any product. it is not caused by teething, and it is not caused by anything you did.
keywords: sleep regression four month night waking

title: Give the baby floor time, not container time
body: a baby on a firm floor builds the strength to roll, sit, and crawl. a baby in a seat or a jumper does not. a blanket on the floor with a few toys is the whole setup. limit swings, bouncers, and jumpers to short stretches. there is no evidence that jumpers help walking and some evidence they delay it.

title: Solids are not yet
body: most babies are ready around six months, when they can sit with support and hold their head steady. starting at four months does not help sleep and does not prevent allergies.

title: Teeth may be close
body: first teeth usually arrive between four and seven months. chewing, drool, and fussiness can start weeks before a tooth appears.

title: Month 5
body: sitting is coming, and so is the first tooth. the six-month visit is next month. your baby is rolling both ways, reaching accurately, and may be sitting with their hands propped in front. they are babbling in long strings and copying sounds. if you are breastfeeding, supply is stable. if you are pumping at work, output often dips on the days you are stressed, and that is not a supply problem. five months is often a good month. sleep may have settled, the baby is fun, and the routine works. notice it, because the next change is coming.

title: Practise sitting with a pillow behind
body: sitting is the skill that unlocks everything after it: reaching, playing, and eventually pulling up. sit the baby on the floor with a nursing pillow or your legs behind them. let them prop on their hands. do not leave them alone, and do not use a seat that holds them upright before they can sit themselves.

title: Know the signs of readiness for solids
body: the six-month visit is where solids get discussed, and the signs are about skills, not about weight or appetite. ready means sitting with little support, holding the head steady, and showing interest in food. tongue thrust that pushes food back out is a sign to wait a few weeks. most babies are ready between five and seven months.

title: Start cleaning the gums and any teeth
body: a tooth that arrives and is not cleaned starts the habit of not cleaning it. wipe the gums with a soft cloth once a day. when a tooth appears, use a soft baby toothbrush with a smear of fluoride toothpaste no bigger than a grain of rice. first dental visit by the first tooth or the first birthday.

title: Separation anxiety starts around now
body: a baby who was happy to be handed over may start to cry when you leave the room. it is a sign of attachment, not a sign of a problem, and it peaks between nine and eighteen months.

title: No water before six months
body: a baby under six months gets all the water they need from milk. extra water can dilute their sodium and is not safe. from six months, a small amount in an open cup with meals is fine.

title: Month 6
body: food starts this month. it is messy, it is slow, and almost none of it is about nutrition yet. most babies can sit with support and are starting to reach and grab. the tongue-thrust reflex fades, which is what makes swallowing possible. teeth may be arriving. if you are breastfeeding, your supply is established and may feel less full. that is normal and not a sign it is dropping. starting solids is the first place where other people's opinions arrive in force. pick a lane and ignore the noise.

title: Start solids, one food at a time
body: around six months, milk alone stops being enough for iron. the first foods matter less than the fact that you start. start with iron-rich foods — pureed meat, beans, or iron-fortified cereal. one new food every few days so you can spot a reaction. milk stays the main source of nutrition until about 12 months; food is practice. no honey before 12 months, no cow's milk as a drink before 12 months, no juice before 12 months, and nothing round and hard. your pediatrician has recommended a different start date for a medical reason. spoon-fed purees baby-led weaning both

title: Get a high chair that is easy to clean
body: you will use it three times a day for two years. the only features that matter are a footrest, a five-point harness, and a tray that goes in the dishwasher. a footrest matters more than it sounds — a baby whose feet dangle cannot sit stably, and unstable sitting makes eating harder. avoid anything with fabric you cannot wipe. do not use a hook-on seat until the baby can sit fully independently. you already have a high chair with a footrest and a harness. ikea antilop stokke tripp trapp a convertible chair

title: Start looking for childcare if you need it
body: waitlists in most us cities run six to eighteen months. six months is the month to get on them, not twelve. ask three questions of every place: what is the staff-to-child ratio, what is the turnover, and can i visit unannounced. licensing records are public in every state — look yours up. naeyc accreditation is a meaningful signal but not the only one. you have childcare arranged, or you are not returning to work. a licensed center a licensed home provider a nanny

title: Water
body: a little water in an open cup with meals is fine from six months. do not give juice, and do not give water in place of milk.

title: Allergens
body: introduce peanut, egg, dairy, wheat, soy, fish, and sesame early and keep them in the diet. delaying them increases the risk of allergy, it does not reduce it.

title: Teeth
body: wipe the gums and any teeth with a soft cloth twice a day. first dental visit by the first tooth or the first birthday, whichever comes first.

title: Sitting
body: sitting with support is not sitting independently. do not leave a baby propped on a bed or sofa.

title: Month 7
body: solids are underway, sitting is nearly there, and the pincer grasp is coming. your baby is sitting with little support, may be starting to crawl or scoot, and is babbling in strings that sound like conversation. they can pass a toy from hand to hand. if you are breastfeeding, your supply adjusts to what the baby takes as solids increase. your period may return now that night feeds are dropping. starting solids is more work than it looks. the mess is the point, and a baby who plays with food is learning.

title: Introduce the common allergens, one at a time
body: early introduction of peanut and egg lowers the chance of allergy, and the window is now rather than later. peanut, egg, milk, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish, sesame, and tree nuts. give one new allergen at a time, in a small amount, at home, in the morning, and wait a few days before the next. keep going with the ones that are fine, because stopping can undo the benefit.

title: Offer soft finger foods for the pincer grasp
body: picking up a small piece of food is the same motion as picking up a cheerio, and it is how the pincer grasp develops. soft cooked vegetable sticks, ripe banana, avocado, scrambled egg, and soft toast strips. cut round things lengthwise, not into coins. sit the baby upright and stay within arm's reach.
keywords: finger food pincer grasp self feeding

title: Babyproof before the baby is mobile
body: a baby who can crawl finds the stairs, the outlets, and the dog bowl in the time it takes to answer a text. anchor furniture to the wall, put covers on outlets, gate the stairs top and bottom, and move cleaning products and medicines out of reach. get down on the floor and look at the room from the baby's height.

title: An open cup is better than a sippy cup
body: from six months, a small amount of water in an open cup with meals helps with oral development. a straw cup is the next best thing. a sippy cup with a valve is the one to skip.

title: Iron matters more now
body: the iron a baby is born with runs low around six months. iron-rich foods are meat, beans, lentils, and fortified cereal. pair them with vitamin c to help absorption.

title: Month 8
body: crawling changes everything. the room is a different room now. your baby is crawling or scooting, pulling to stand, and sitting without support. they can pick up a small piece of food with a thumb and finger and are starting to understand that things still exist when they cannot see them. if you are breastfeeding, supply adjusts to what the baby takes. your period may be back. your back may be feeling the lifting more than it did. a mobile baby is more work and more fun. the babyproofing is not optional now, and it is easier to do it in one afternoon than one emergency at a time.

title: Babyproof the room the baby is in, not the whole house
body: a crawling baby finds the one thing you missed. doing the room they are in first is what actually protects them this week. anchor every bookshelf and dresser to the wall. cover outlets. gate the stairs at the top and the bottom. move medicines, cleaning products, and small objects above counter height. get on the floor and look.

title: Know that separation anxiety is a sign of attachment
body: a baby who cries when you leave the room is showing that they know you are a specific person and that they want you. that is the goal, not a problem. it peaks between nine and eighteen months. a short goodbye is better than a sneaky exit. a consistent caregiver and a predictable routine help more than anything else.

title: Give the baby space to move
body: crawling is built by crawling. a baby in a seat or a jumper is not practising it. clear a floor space and let them go. put a toy just out of reach. limit containers to short stretches. bare feet on a firm floor give better traction than socks.

title: Pulling to stand comes before walking
body: most babies pull to stand between eight and ten months and walk between eleven and fifteen months. a baby who is not pulling up by twelve months is worth mentioning at the visit.

title: An open cup is still better
body: a small amount of water in an open cup with meals. a straw cup is the next best. a valve sippy cup teaches a suck that does not help speech.

title: Month 9
body: the nine-month visit is this month. it is the one where the doctor watches the baby move, not just measures them. your baby is crawling well, pulling to stand, and may be cruising along furniture. they can pick up a pea with a thumb and finger and are starting to copy sounds and gestures. if you are breastfeeding, supply is stable. if you are not, the baby is eating more food and drinking less milk, which is the direction of travel. nine months is often when the baby's personality arrives in full. it is also when the house needs a second look, because the baby is faster than last month.

title: Go to the nine-month visit
body: this visit checks movement, hearing, and development, and it is where a concern is easiest to raise. the nine-month visit usually has no vaccines. the doctor will watch the baby sit, crawl, and pick things up. ask about movement, hearing, and whether the baby is saying consonant sounds. write your questions down before you go.

title: Move toward three meals and two snacks
body: by nine months, food is becoming nutrition rather than practice, and the rhythm of meals is what makes the next year easier. three meals and two snacks, with milk around them rather than instead of them. offer iron-rich food at two of the meals. let the baby feed themselves, even when it is slow.

title: Let the baby cruise along the furniture
body: cruising is the bridge between pulling up and walking, and it is built by doing it. line up sturdy furniture with small gaps. put a toy on the far end. bare feet. do not hold both hands and walk them, because that teaches a posture they cannot use alone.

title: First words are close
body: most babies say a first word between ten and fourteen months. babbling with consonants at nine months is the thing that comes before it.

title: A nine-month sleep wobble is common
body: crawling, standing, and separation anxiety all arrive at once, and sleep often gets worse before it gets better. it is developmental and it passes.

title: Month 10
body: standing, cruising, and the first real word. the first birthday is two months away. your baby is pulling to stand, cruising, and may be standing alone for a few seconds. they understand simple words and can follow a point. if you are breastfeeding, the baby is likely down to a few feeds a day. your body adjusts. if you are not, the transition to whole milk is a conversation for the twelve-month visit. ten months is when the baby starts to have opinions about food, sleep, and being put down. that is a good sign, and it is also tiring.

title: Talk to the baby constantly, and name what you do
body: language is built by hearing it, and the words that stick are the ones attached to something happening. narrate the day: now we are washing your hands, cold water. read the same few books until they are boring. pause and let the baby babble back. screen time does not do this, and background television does the opposite.

title: Know the plan for milk at twelve months
body: the twelve-month visit is where the switch from formula or breast milk to whole milk gets decided, and it is easier if you know the options. whole milk from twelve months, in an open cup, two to three cups a day. not before twelve months. if the baby is still breastfeeding, that can continue. plant milks are not a straight swap unless they are fortified and the doctor agrees.
keywords: whole milk twelve months cow milk

title: Let the baby walk barefoot indoors
body: bare feet give better feedback than shoes, and the feedback is what builds balance. bare feet on a firm floor indoors. shoes are for outside, and they should be flexible with a thin sole. a baby who is not walking by fifteen months is worth mentioning at the visit.

title: The first birthday is a party for you
body: the baby will not remember it. keep it small, keep it short, and do not schedule it over a nap. one candle and a mess of cake is the whole tradition.

title: Teeth need cleaning twice a day
body: a smear of fluoride toothpaste no bigger than a grain of rice, twice a day, from the first tooth. first dental visit by the first tooth or the first birthday.

title: Month 11
body: the twelve-month visit is next month, and it is the one with the most decisions in it. your baby is standing, may be taking first steps, and can say one or two words. they understand no and can follow a simple instruction. if you are breastfeeding, you may be down to morning and night feeds. if you are formula feeding, you are close to the end of it. eleven months is when the first birthday planning starts, and when the twelve-month visit questions start to matter. write them down now.

title: Book the twelve-month visit
body: this is the visit with the most decisions: vaccines, the switch to whole milk, and the developmental check. the us schedule at twelve months is mmr, varicella, hib, and pcv, and hepatitis a and b depending on what was given earlier. ask about whole milk, iron, and whether the baby needs a lead test. ask about walking if they are not yet.

title: Plan the switch to whole milk
body: the switch is a change of habit as much as a change of drink, and doing it over a week is easier than doing it overnight. whole milk from twelve months, two to three cups a day, in an open cup. mix it with formula over a week if the baby refuses it. do not add it to a bottle at bedtime, because that is the habit that causes tooth decay.

title: Give the baby something to push
body: a push toy gives a baby who is not yet confident the balance to take steps. a sturdy push wagon or a laundry basket with something heavy in it. not a baby walker with wheels and a seat, which is banned in canada and associated with injuries here.

title: Ask about a lead test
body: the cdc recommends a blood lead test for children at twelve months in many areas, and the pediatrician will know whether yours is one. lead has no symptoms at low levels.

title: Drop the bottle by twelve months
body: prolonged bottle use is linked to tooth decay and to iron deficiency from too much milk. twelve months is the usual time to move to an open cup and a straw cup.

title: Month 12
body: one year. the first birthday is a real milestone, and the next stage starts next month. your baby may be walking or close to it, says a few words, and can follow simple instructions. they are starting to test what happens when they do something you said not to. if you are breastfeeding, you can keep going for as long as you both want. if you are formula feeding, the switch to whole milk happens now. a year is a long time and you did it. the toddler stage is different: more opinion, more movement, and the same amount of love.

title: Go to the twelve-month visit
body: this is the visit with the most decisions in it, and the one where the next year's schedule gets set. the us schedule at twelve months is mmr, varicella, hib, and pcv, and hepatitis a and b depending on what was given earlier. ask about whole milk, iron, and a lead test. ask about walking and words if either is behind.

title: Switch to whole milk and drop the bottle
body: whole milk has the fat a one-year-old needs, and the bottle is the habit that causes tooth decay after a year. two to three cups a day, in an open cup or a straw cup. mix with formula over a week if needed. no bottle at bedtime. milk is a drink, not a meal replacement, so it comes with food rather than instead of it.

title: Know that tantrums are starting, and they are not defiance
body: a one-year-old has big feelings and no words for them. the behaviour is the communication, not a challenge to your authority. name the feeling, stay nearby, and do not try to reason with a screaming toddler. it peaks between eighteen months and three years. hitting and biting are common and are handled by a calm no and a redirect, not by punishment.

title: The toddler stage starts next month
body: the guide switches from months to the toddler timeline. the cadence slows down, because a month is a long time at this age.

title: First dental visit by the first birthday
body: a check by the first tooth or the first birthday, whichever comes first. it is short, it is mostly a look, and it sets up the habit.

title: Month 13
body: the guide changes shape here. a month is a long time at this age, so the steps are fewer and they matter more. your child is walking, or close to it, and can say a few words. they understand much more than they can say, and they are starting to test what happens when they do something you said not to. if you are breastfeeding, you can keep going for as long as you both want. if you were formula feeding, the switch to whole milk happened last month. the first year is over and you did it. the second year is different: more opinion, more movement, and the same amount of love.

title: Know that a tantrum is not defiance
body: a one-year-old has big feelings and almost no words for them. the behaviour is the communication. name the feeling, stay nearby, and do not try to reason with a screaming child. it peaks between eighteen months and three years. hitting and biting are common and are handled by a calm no and a redirect, not by punishment.

title: Watch for the move to one nap
body: most children drop to one nap between twelve and eighteen months, and the sign is a second nap that pushes bedtime too late. the usual pattern is a morning nap that gets shorter and a long afternoon nap. if the second nap is still happening at four in the afternoon and bedtime is a fight, drop it and move lunch earlier.

title: Let them walk barefoot indoors
body: bare feet give better feedback than shoes, and the feedback is what builds balance. bare feet on a firm floor indoors. shoes are for outside, and they should be flexible with a thin sole. a child who is not walking by eighteen months is worth mentioning at the visit.

title: Whole milk until two
body: whole milk, two to three cups a day, until the second birthday. after two, the fat can come down to 2% if the child is eating well. milk is a drink, not a meal replacement.

title: A dental visit by the first birthday
body: a check by the first tooth or the first birthday, whichever came first. it is short, it is mostly a look, and it sets up the habit.

title: Month 14
body: words are coming. the fifteen-month visit is next month, and it is the one where language gets counted. your child is walking well, climbing onto low furniture, and can say several words. they point at what they want and look back at you to check you saw it. your back and knees are doing more work than they did a year ago. lifting a walking child is a different movement than lifting a baby. fourteen months is when the child starts to have a plan. it is also when the house needs a second look, because they can now reach things they could not last month.

title: Book the fifteen-month visit
body: this is the next vaccine set and the visit where the doctor counts words and watches the child walk. the us schedule at fifteen months is dtap, hib, pcv, mmr, varicella, and hepatitis a and b depending on what was given earlier. write down the words the child says so you can answer the question accurately.

title: Count the words, and write them down
body: a list of the words your child says is the single most useful thing you can bring to the fifteen-month visit. at fifteen months, most children say a few words beyond mama and dada. they do not have to be clear. write down every word you have heard, including the ones only you understand, and bring the list.

title: Get shoes that bend
body: a stiff shoe changes how a new walker moves, and a new walker is still learning the movement. the shoe should bend where the foot bends, have a thin sole, and leave room at the toe. check the fit every two months, because toddler feet grow in bursts. bare feet indoors is still better.

title: Pointing is a language milestone
body: pointing at something and looking back at you is a shared-attention skill, and it comes before words. a child who does not point by eighteen months is worth mentioning at the visit.

title: Climbing starts before you expect it
body: a child who can walk can usually climb onto a low chair. anchor the furniture, and move the things you do not want reached one shelf higher than you think is necessary.

title: Month 15
body: the fifteen-month visit is this month. it is the one where the doctor counts words. your child is walking, may be running, and says several words. they can follow a simple instruction without a gesture, and they are starting to help with dressing by holding out an arm. if you are pregnant again, the lifting is the thing to watch. if you are not, nothing about your body changes this month. fifteen months is often when the gap between what the child wants and what they can say gets widest. that gap is what tantrums are made of.

title: Go to the fifteen-month visit
body: this is the vaccine set and the developmental check where language, walking, and pointing all get looked at. the us schedule at fifteen months is dtap, hib, pcv, mmr, varicella, and hepatitis a and b depending on what was given earlier. bring the word list. ask about the autism screen, which is done at eighteen and twenty-four months.

title: Respond to a tantrum the same way every time
body: a predictable response is what teaches a child that the feeling is survivable, and it is easier to do when you have decided in advance. get low, say what you see, and wait. do not negotiate during the tantrum, and do not leave. talk about it afterwards, when the child is calm, in one sentence. the same response every time is the whole method.

title: Read the same book until it is boring
body: repetition is how a fifteen-month-old learns words, and a familiar book is where they start to fill in the gaps. read the same three or four books for a month. pause before the last word of a line and let the child fill it in. point at the pictures and name them. a new book every night is less useful than one book ten times.

title: First molars arrive around now
body: the first molars usually come between thirteen and nineteen months, and they are bigger than the front teeth. chewing, drool, and night waking can come with them.

title: Screens are not a language teacher
body: a child under two learns language from a person, not from a screen. video calls with a grandparent are the exception, because someone is responding. background television is the thing to turn off.

title: Month 16
body: the vocabulary is growing faster than you can count it, and the spoon is the next skill. your child says new words most weeks, can walk backwards, and is starting to run. they can point to a few body parts and follow a two-step instruction. if you are carrying a sixteen-month-old, the hip carry is the one that hurts. switch sides, and use a stroller for the long walks. sixteen months is often a good month. the walking works, the words are coming, and the routine holds. notice it.

title: Let them use a spoon, even badly
body: self-feeding with a spoon is a skill that takes months, and it only develops if the child is allowed to do it. give a spoon and a thick food like yogurt or mashed potato, which stays on. expect the floor to be involved. offer a loaded spoon to start, then let them load it. do not take the spoon away to finish the job faster.

title: Give two-step instructions
body: following two steps is a language and memory skill, and it is built by doing it in play rather than in a test. put the cup on the table. bring me the ball. keep it playful and give the child time to work it out. if they do one step, repeat the second rather than the whole thing.

title: Brush twice a day, and mean it
body: a toddler cannot brush their own teeth well enough, and the habit is easier to build now than at three. a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste, twice a day, with you finishing the job. lie the child down or stand behind them. a timer or a song helps. first dental visit if it has not happened yet.

title: Picky eating starts around now
body: appetite drops in the second year because growth slows. a child who ate everything at eleven months may refuse it at sixteen. keep offering without pressure, and do not make a second meal.

title: Too much milk crowds out food
body: more than about sixteen to twenty ounces of milk a day leaves no room for iron-rich food, and it is a common cause of low iron in toddlers.

title: Month 17
body: the eighteen-month visit is next month, and it is the one with the autism screen in it. your child is running, climbing, and can say around ten words. they can point to several body parts and are starting to show you things rather than just wanting them. separation anxiety often peaks around now. leaving the room can be a crisis, and that is a sign of attachment rather than a problem. seventeen months is when the child's opinion arrives in full. it is a good sign and it is tiring.

title: Book the eighteen-month visit
body: this is the visit with the autism screen, the next vaccine set, and the language check. the us schedule at eighteen months is dtap and hepatitis a, with others depending on what was given earlier. the doctor will do a formal autism screen, usually the m-chat. write down the words and the gestures the child uses.

title: Anchor the furniture, all of it
body: a seventeen-month-old can climb onto a chair, and a dresser that tips is the injury that follows. anchor every bookshelf, dresser, and television to the wall. move the changing table away from the window. put the stool where it cannot be used to reach the counter. this is a one-afternoon job that prevents a specific and serious injury.

title: Make goodbyes short and the same
body: a predictable goodbye is easier than a disappearing parent, even when the goodbye is loud. say the same words every time, leave, and do not come back for one more hug. a caregiver who distracts the child after you go is helping. sneaking out teaches the child that you can vanish.

title: Ten to twenty words is typical at eighteen months
body: most children say ten to twenty words at eighteen months and understand far more. a child with fewer than six words at eighteen months is worth raising at the visit rather than waiting.

title: The canine teeth come next
body: after the first molars, the canines usually arrive between sixteen and twenty-two months. the second molars are the last, around two to three years.

title: Month 18
body: the eighteen-month visit is this month. it is the one with the autism screen, and it is a conversation, not a verdict. your child is running, may be climbing stairs with a hand held, and says around ten to twenty words. they can point to three or more body parts and are starting to pretend, like feeding a doll. if you are pregnant again, eighteen months is the age gap that is hardest on the body. ask for help with the lifting. the autism screen is a questionnaire, not a diagnosis. a positive screen means a closer look, and a closer look early is the thing that helps.

title: Go to the eighteen-month visit
body: this is the autism screen, the next vaccine set, and the language check, and it is the visit where a concern is easiest to raise. the us schedule at eighteen months is dtap and hepatitis a, with others depending on what was given earlier. the screen is usually the m-chat, eighteen questions. answer them about what the child does, not what you hope they do. a referral for an evaluation is not a diagnosis.

title: Name everything, all day
body: vocabulary at this age grows from hearing words attached to things that are happening. narrate what you are doing and what the child is doing. expand what they say: if they say dog, say yes, a big brown dog. read the same books. sing the same songs. screen time does not do this.

title: Decide your limits before the tantrum
body: a limit that changes depending on how loud the child is teaches that loud works. pick the few things that are non-negotiable and hold them every time. everything else can be a choice between two options, which is what a toddler actually wants. say the limit once, calmly, and then stop talking.

title: Pretend play starts now
body: feeding a doll, stirring a pot, and putting a toy to bed are the beginnings of pretend play, and they are a language and social milestone.

title: Stairs need a gate until three
body: a child can climb stairs with a hand held at eighteen months but cannot be trusted on them alone until around three. gate the top and the bottom.

title: Month 19
body: two words together is the next milestone, and it is closer than it looks. your child says around twenty words and is starting to put two together, like more milk or daddy gone. they can run, kick a ball, and climb onto a chair. if you are carrying a nineteen-month-old, your shoulder is doing the work your back used to. switch sides and use the stroller for the long walks. nineteen months is when the child starts to negotiate. it is a good sign, and it is the reason a choice between two things works better than an instruction.

title: Model two words together
body: two-word phrases are the next language step, and they come from hearing them rather than from being asked to repeat them. when the child says one word, give it back with two: milk becomes more milk, up becomes up please. do not correct, just expand. most children put two words together between eighteen and twenty-four months.

title: Decide the screen rule now, before it is a fight
body: a rule set at nineteen months is easier to hold than a rule set at three, when the child can argue. for a child under two, the recommendation is no solo screen time other than video calls. if you use a screen, watch it together and talk about it. background television is the thing to turn off, because it costs language even when nobody is watching.

title: Brush twice a day, and finish the job yourself
body: a toddler can hold a brush but cannot clean the back teeth, and the habit is what carries into the years when they can. a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste, twice a day. let them have a turn, then take it and finish. lying down or standing behind works better than facing them. a two-minute song is a better timer than a threat.

title: Picky eating is a stage, not a verdict
body: appetite drops in the second year because growth slows. keep offering the food without pressure, eat together, and do not make a second meal. a child may need to see a food fifteen times before eating it.

title: Iron is the nutrient to watch
body: milk displaces iron-rich food. keep milk to about sixteen ounces a day, and offer meat, beans, lentils, and fortified cereal. low iron shows up as tiredness and irritability, not as a symptom you would notice.

title: Month 20
body: pretend play is starting, and it is the best language tool you have. your child is running, can walk up stairs with a hand held, and says around twenty to fifty words. they are starting to pretend, like stirring a pot or putting a toy to bed. your body has been carrying a growing child for twenty months. if something hurts, it is worth a physio visit rather than a wait. twenty months is when the child's play becomes a window into what they understand. watching it is more useful than any checklist.

title: Play pretend with them, and follow their lead
body: pretend play is where language, memory, and social understanding come together, and it works best when the child is the one deciding. sit on the floor and copy what they do. if they stir a pot, stir a pot. add one idea, not five. a box is a car, a spoon is a phone. do not correct the game, join it.

title: Book the two-year visit
body: the two-year visit is the second autism screen and the next developmental check, and the good slots go early. the two-year visit usually has no vaccines if the eighteen-month set is complete. the doctor will do a second autism screen and check language, movement, and teeth. write down the words and the two-word phrases.

title: Teach the stairs, and keep the gate
body: a child can learn to go down stairs backwards on their tummy long before they can do it on their feet. practise going down on the tummy, feet first, with you below. keep the gates at the top and the bottom. a child is not safe on stairs alone until around three.

title: The second molars are the last teeth
body: second molars usually arrive between twenty-three and thirty-three months, and they are the ones that wake a child at night. the full set of baby teeth is complete around three.

title: Sharing is not a two-year-old skill
body: a two-year-old is not developmentally able to share. parallel play, side by side with the same toys, is the goal. taking turns with a timer works better than asking for a share.

title: Month 21
body: running, kicking, and climbing. the body is ahead of the words, and that is the right order. your child runs well, can kick a ball forward, and walks up stairs with a hand held. they say around fifty words and are starting to put two together. if you are pregnant again, twenty-one months is the age gap where the lifting gets hard. ask for help rather than pushing through. twenty-one months is often when the child starts to help. let them, even when it is slower.

title: Let them help, even when it is slower
body: helping is how a child learns to be part of a household, and the willingness to help peaks before the ability. put the laundry in the basket together. hand them a cloth to wipe the table. let them stir. it takes three times as long and it is the whole point. a child who helps at two is a child who helps at four.

title: Kick and roll a ball every day
body: kicking a ball is a balance and coordination skill, and it is the foundation for running, jumping, and sport. roll a ball back and forth sitting down first, then standing. kick a soft ball indoors. a child who can kick forward at two is on track. do not correct the foot, just play.

title: Know the water rules before summer
body: drowning is the leading cause of injury death in children one to four, and it is silent. a child this age needs an adult within arm's reach in any water, including a bathtub and a paddling pool. empty the paddling pool after every use. a fence with a self-closing gate around a pool is the thing that works.

title: Two words is enough for now
body: two-word phrases between eighteen and twenty-four months are on track. three words usually come between twenty-four and thirty months. a child with no two-word phrases at twenty-four months is worth raising at the visit.

title: One nap is the norm now
body: most children are on one nap by twenty-one months, usually after lunch, for one to two hours. a child who still needs two is not behind.

title: Month 22
body: fifty words, two-word phrases, and an opinion about getting dressed. your child says around fifty words, puts two together, and can follow a two-step instruction. they can take off some clothes and are starting to try to put them on. if you are still breastfeeding, that is fine. if you stopped a year ago, that is fine too. there is no milestone for this. twenty-two months is when the child starts to have a preference about clothes, food, and which cup. that is a good sign, and it is easier to work with than against.

title: Let them dress themselves, badly
body: dressing is a self-care skill that takes a year to learn, and it only develops if the child is allowed to try. start with the easy things: taking off socks, pulling up trousers, pushing an arm through a sleeve. lay the clothes out in the order they go on. give extra time in the morning rather than doing it for them.

title: Offer two choices, not an open question
body: a two-year-old can decide between two things and cannot decide between everything, and the open question is what starts a tantrum. do you want the red cup or the blue cup. do you want to walk or be carried. both options are ones you can live with. an open question at this age is a request for a fight.

title: Read every day, and let them choose the book
body: reading is the single most reliable language input at this age, and choosing the book is what keeps them in it. two books before bed, and the child picks. read the same ones as often as they want. point at pictures and ask what happens next. a child who is read to every day hears about a million more words a year than one who is not.

title: The canines are the last of the front teeth
body: canines usually arrive between sixteen and twenty-two months. the second molars come last, between twenty-three and thirty-three months.

title: Check the shoe size every two months
body: toddler feet grow in bursts, and a shoe that fit in spring may be tight by summer. check the toe room with your thumb, and check for redness after a long walk.

title: Month 23
body: the two-year visit is next month. it is the second autism screen, and the last one before school. your child says fifty or more words, puts two together, and can run and climb. they are starting to sort shapes and colors and can follow a two-step instruction. if you are pregnant again, the two-year gap is the one where the lifting and the naps collide. ask for help now rather than at thirty-eight weeks. twenty-three months is the last month before the check that everyone talks about. write the questions down now, because the visit is short.

title: Book the two-year visit
body: this is the second autism screen, the language check, and the visit where a concern is easiest to raise. the two-year visit usually has no vaccines if the eighteen-month set is complete. the doctor will do a second autism screen and check language, movement, teeth, and growth. bring the word list and the two-word phrases.

title: Know the signs of potty readiness, and do not start early
body: starting before the child is ready makes the whole thing take longer, and the signs are behavioural rather than about age. ready means staying dry for two hours, telling you when they have gone, showing interest in the toilet, and being able to pull trousers down. most children are ready between two and three. starting at eighteen months because a book said so is the common mistake.

title: Watch for the second molars
body: the second molars are the largest teeth and the ones that wake a child at night, and they arrive around now. chewing on fingers, drool, night waking, and a low fever can come with them. a fever over 100.4°f is not teething and is worth a call. a cold teether and a dose of pain relief at the right weight is the whole treatment.

title: Twelve hours at night and one nap
body: a two-year-old usually sleeps eleven to fourteen hours in a day, including one nap of one to two hours. a child who is fighting the nap may be ready to drop it, but most are not until three.

title: Whole milk until two, then 2% is fine
body: after the second birthday, the fat can come down to 2% if the child is eating well. keep it to about sixteen ounces a day so it does not crowd out food.

title: Month 24
body: two years. the two-year visit is this month, and it is the second autism screen. your child says fifty or more words, puts two together, and can run, kick, and climb. they can follow a two-step instruction and are starting to sort by shape and color. two years of carrying a child is two years of a body doing more than it did before. if something hurts, it is worth a physio visit. two is a real milestone and it is worth noticing. the next year is the year of sentences, and it is easier than the year of tantrums.

title: Go to the two-year visit
body: this is the second autism screen, the language check, and the visit where the next year's schedule gets set. the two-year visit usually has no vaccines if the eighteen-month set is complete. the doctor will do a second autism screen and check language, movement, teeth, and growth. ask about the next visit, which is at thirty months.

title: Model three words together
body: three-word sentences usually arrive between twenty-four and thirty months, and they come from hearing them. when the child says two words, give three back: more milk becomes more milk please. ask questions that need more than yes or no. narrate what you are doing. do not correct, expand.

title: Put a potty in the bathroom, and do not push it
body: a potty that is just there, with no pressure, is what makes the later attempt quick. put a potty in the bathroom the child uses. let them sit on it clothed if they want. talk about what the toilet is for. do not start training until the child shows the readiness signs, which for most is between two and three.

title: Milk comes down to about sixteen ounces
body: after two, whole milk is no longer needed and 2% is fine. keep it to about sixteen ounces a day, in a cup, with meals.

title: Two is when the screen rules get tested
body: the recommendation for two to five is no more than an hour a day of high-quality content, watched with an adult. a child who has had no screens until two will ask for them now, because they see them everywhere.

title: Month 25
body: sentences are coming, and the second molars are on their way. your child says two or three words together, can run and jump in place, and is starting to play next to other children rather than with them. if you are pregnant again, the twenty-five-month-old is heavy and wants to be carried. a stroller is not a failure. twenty-five months is when the child starts to play with other children rather than beside them. it is slow, and it is the beginning of friendship.

title: Arrange play with one other child, not a group
body: parallel play turns into cooperative play through repetition with the same child, and a group is too much at this age. one other child, a short visit, and a shared activity like water or blocks. expect them to play side by side and to fight over one toy. that is the stage. do not force a share.

title: Watch for the second molars
body: the second molars are the last baby teeth and the ones that wake a child at night, and they arrive around now. chewing, drool, night waking, and a low fever can come with them. a fever over 100.4°f is not teething. a cold teether and pain relief at the right weight is the whole treatment.

title: Ask questions that need more than yes
