body: a question with a yes or no answer gets one word. a question that starts with what or where gets a sentence. what did you see at the park. where is your shoe. what is the dog doing. wait for the answer, even when the wait is long. answering your own question teaches the child that the wait is not worth it.

title: Counting comes before the numbers mean anything
body: a two-year-old can recite one, two, three without understanding quantity. counting objects by touching them is the step that makes the numbers mean something, and it comes around three.

title: Colors are a three-year-old skill
body: most children can name a color by three and sort by color earlier. asking a two-year-old what color something is and getting it wrong is not a problem.

title: Month 26
body: the thirty-month visit is next month, and it is a short one. your child says three words together, can jump with both feet off the floor, and can turn a page of a book. they are starting to sort by shape and color. if you are pregnant again, the last trimester with a two-year-old is the hardest stretch. ask for help with the lifting now. twenty-six months is when the child starts to have a memory for what happened yesterday. that is what makes a routine comforting rather than just familiar.

title: Book the thirty-month visit
body: this is a short developmental check, and it is the visit where a language or movement concern is easiest to raise. the thirty-month visit usually has no vaccines. the doctor will check language, movement, and teeth, and will ask about sleep and eating. write down the sentences the child says so you can answer accurately.

title: Practise jumping
body: jumping with both feet off the floor is a two-year-old milestone, and it is built by doing it. jump off a low step holding hands, then alone. jump on a bed with you there. jump over a line on the floor. a child who cannot jump by thirty months is worth mentioning at the visit.

title: Keep the bedtime routine the same
body: a predictable routine is what makes bedtime work at two, and it is easier to hold than to rebuild. the same three or four steps in the same order, about twenty minutes, ending in the bed. bath, teeth, two books, song, bed. a visual schedule on the wall helps a child who cannot read.

title: Three words is on track
body: three-word sentences between twenty-four and thirty months are on track. a child who is not putting three words together by thirty months is worth raising at the visit.

title: The full set of baby teeth is complete around three
body: twenty teeth, with the second molars last. a dental visit every six months from now is the usual schedule.

title: Month 27
body: three words together, and a tricycle is the next thing. your child says three words together, can jump with both feet, and can walk up stairs alternating feet with a hand held. they are starting to use a spoon and fork together. if you are carrying a twenty-seven-month-old, your back has been doing this for over two years. a physio visit is not an indulgence. twenty-seven months is when the child starts to tell you what happened. the stories are short and mostly about the dog, and they are the beginning of narrative.

title: Get a tricycle, or a balance bike
body: pedalling is a coordination skill that comes before riding, and a balance bike teaches the balance that a tricycle does not. a tricycle with pedals is the traditional first step. a balance bike skips the pedals and teaches balance first, which most children find easier. either is fine. a helmet from the first ride, every time.

title: Let them use a fork, and expect it to be slow
body: using a fork is a fine-motor skill that takes a year, and it only develops if the child is allowed to do it. a small fork with rounded tines. stab a piece and hand it over to start. expect the food to be dropped and the meal to take longer. do not take the fork away to finish faster.

title: A helmet from the first ride
body: a helmet that is not worn from the first ride is a helmet that is fought over at four. fit it so it sits level, two fingers above the eyebrow, with the strap snug under the chin. wear one yourself. a child who sees a helmet on every ride does not question it.

title: Ask what happened, not what they did
body: a child who is asked what happened at the park will tell a story. a child who is asked if they had fun will say yes. the first builds language, the second does not.

title: The nap is still needed
body: most two-year-olds still need one nap of one to two hours. dropping it early makes the evening worse, not better.

title: Month 28
body: the why questions start now, and they are not a test. your child says three words together, can follow a two-step instruction, and is starting to use words like i, me, and you. they can name a few body parts and a few colors. if you are pregnant again, the last weeks with a two-year-old are a logistics problem more than a physical one. line up help for the birth. the why questions are the child working out how the world fits together. they are not asking for a lecture, and they are not testing you.

title: Answer the why questions, briefly
body: a short answer keeps the conversation going. a long one ends it, and the child stops asking. why is the sky blue. because sunlight has colors in it and the blue ones bounce around the most. that is enough. if you do not know, say you do not know and look it up together. the asking is the point.

title: Let them dress themselves, all of it
body: dressing is a self-care skill that takes a year, and a child who can do it at three is a child who is ready for preschool. lay the clothes out in order. start with the easy things: trousers, then a t-shirt, then socks. buttons and zips come later. give ten extra minutes rather than doing it for them.

title: Try potty learning if the signs are there
body: the signs matter more than the age, and a child who is ready learns in days rather than months. ready means staying dry for two hours, telling you when they have gone, pulling trousers down, and showing interest. pick a week with no travel. expect accidents. do not go back to nappies during the day once you start.

title: Two hundred words is typical at two and a half
body: most children have around two hundred to three hundred words at thirty months and are putting three together. a child with far fewer is worth raising at the visit.

title: An hour a day, watched together
body: the recommendation for two to five is no more than an hour a day of high-quality content, watched with an adult who talks about it. a screen alone in a room is the thing to avoid.

title: Month 29
body: the thirty-month visit is next month. it is short, and it is the last one before three. your child says three words together, can jump, and is starting to run around obstacles. they can name a friend and are beginning to take turns with help. if you are pregnant again, the birth plan needs a plan for the two-year-old. who takes them, and where. twenty-nine months is when the child starts to have a friend rather than a playmate. it is a small and real thing.

title: Book the thirty-month visit
body: this is a short developmental check, and it is the last visit before the three-year check. the thirty-month visit usually has no vaccines. the doctor will check language, movement, and teeth, and will ask about sleep, eating, and toilet learning. write the questions down before you go.

title: Practise taking turns with a timer
body: taking turns is a skill that is taught, and a timer makes the waiting concrete in a way that a sentence does not. use a two-minute timer. one child has the toy until it rings, then the other. stay close and narrate. a two-year-old cannot wait long, so keep the turns short. this is the foundation for sharing at three.

title: Teach their own name
body: knowing their own name is a safety skill as well as a language one, and it is what a preschool teacher will ask for. say the name in songs and in play. ask who is this in the mirror. point at their photo. a child who can say their first name by three is on track. a surname comes later.

title: A dental visit every six months
body: from two, a check every six months is the usual schedule. a first visit may have happened already; if not, it is worth booking now.

title: Eleven to fourteen hours, including the nap
body: a two-and-a-half-year-old usually sleeps eleven to fourteen hours a day, including one nap. night waking is still common and is not a sign of a problem.

title: Month 30
body: two and a half. the thirty-month visit is this month, and the next one is at three. your child says three words together, can jump with both feet, and can walk up stairs alternating feet with a hand held. they can name a friend and are starting to take turns. if you are pregnant again, thirty months is the gap where the older child can help. let them. thirty months is when the child's play gets a plot. it is the best thing to watch, and it is the thing to protect time for.

title: Go to the thirty-month visit
body: this is a short developmental check, and it is the last visit before the three-year check. the thirty-month visit usually has no vaccines. the doctor will check language, movement, and teeth, and will ask about sleep, eating, and toilet learning. ask about preschool and about the three-year visit.

title: Practise stairs, alternating feet
body: alternating feet on stairs is a thirty-month milestone, and it is built by doing it with a hand held. walk up and down with a hand held, and say the feet out loud. a child who is still going up one foot at a time at thirty months is not behind, but it is worth practising. keep the gates until three.

title: Give the pretend play a plot
body: pretend play with a sequence is what builds narrative, and narrative is what reading comprehension is made of. set up a scene: the teddy is sick, the doctor comes, the teddy gets better. let the child direct. add one prop, not five. ask what happens next. this is the work of a two-and-a-half-year-old.

title: Preschool starts thinking now
body: most preschools take children from two and a half or three. ask about ratios, staff turnover, and how they handle a child who is upset. a visit tells you more than a brochure.

title: The nap may be ending, but not yet
body: most children drop the nap between three and four. a child who is fighting the nap at thirty months is more likely overtired than ready to drop it.

title: Month 31
body: the three-year visit is two months away, and it is the last one in this guide. your child says three or four words together, can jump, and can walk up stairs alternating feet. they are starting to use words like because and and, and they can follow a three-step instruction. if you are pregnant again, the last weeks with a two-and-a-half-year-old are a logistics problem. line up who takes them. thirty-one months is when the child starts to argue. it is a language milestone wearing a difficult hat.

title: Book the three-year visit
body: this is the last visit in this guide, and it is the one where preschool readiness and language get checked. the three-year visit usually has no vaccines if the eighteen-month set is complete. the doctor will check language, movement, teeth, and growth, and will ask about preschool. write the questions down now.

title: Let them argue, and hold the limit
body: an argument is a child practising reasoning, and the limit is what makes the practice safe. hear the argument out, then say the limit once. you can be persuaded by a good reason and still hold a limit that is not negotiable. do not argue back, and do not change the limit because the argument was loud.

title: Introduce scissors, with supervision
body: cutting is a fine-motor skill that comes before writing, and it is taught rather than discovered. blunt-tip child scissors and strips of paper. show how to hold them, then let the child snip. stay close. a child who can cut a strip at three is on track. do not use scissors as a reward or a punishment.

title: A thousand words by three
body: most children have around a thousand words by three and speak in sentences of three or more. a child who is not understood by strangers at three is worth raising at the visit.

title: Visit before you choose
body: ask about ratios, staff turnover, how they handle a child who is upset, and what a typical day looks like. a visit tells you more than a brochure, and a second visit tells you more than the first.

title: Month 32
body: preschool is a decision this year, and the good places fill early. your child speaks in sentences of three or more words, can jump, and can pedal a tricycle. they can name a friend and are starting to play with other children rather than beside them. if you are pregnant again, the birth plan needs a plan for the older child. who takes them, where they go, and for how long. thirty-two months is when the child starts to have a life outside the house. that is the point of preschool, and it is also the thing that makes the first drop-off hard.

title: Visit three preschools before you choose
body: a preschool is a place your child will spend a thousand hours in, and a brochure cannot tell you what the room feels like. visit at drop-off, not at tour time. ask about ratios, staff turnover, how they handle a child who is upset, and what happens when a child bites. ask what a typical day looks like. trust the feeling in the room.

title: Teach them to write their name, or the first letter
body: writing a name is a three-to-four-year-old skill, and the first letter is where it starts. write the name in big letters and let the child trace it with a finger, then a crayon. start with the first letter. do not correct the grip yet. a child who can recognise their name at three is on track.

title: Finish potty learning before preschool starts
body: most preschools expect a child to be out of nappies by three, and the summer before is the easiest time to do it. pick a week with no travel. expect accidents. do not go back to nappies during the day once you start. night dryness comes later and is not part of it.

title: The nap may be ending
body: most children drop the nap between three and four. a child who is fighting the nap at thirty-two months is more likely overtired than ready to drop it. quiet time in the afternoon is the bridge.

title: Twenty teeth, and a check every six months
body: the full set of baby teeth is complete around three. a dental check every six months from now is the usual schedule.

title: Month 33
body: the three-year visit is next month. it is the last one in this guide. your child speaks in sentences, can jump, pedal, and climb. they can follow a three-step instruction and are starting to understand the idea of yesterday and tomorrow. if you are pregnant again, the three-year gap is the one where the older child can understand that a baby is coming. tell them early and simply. thirty-three months is when the child starts to ask about the baby, or about the world, in a way that has an answer. answer it.

title: Book the three-year visit
body: this is the last visit in this guide, and it is the one where preschool readiness and language get checked. the three-year visit usually has no vaccines if the eighteen-month set is complete. the doctor will check language, movement, teeth, and growth, and will ask about preschool and toilet learning. bring the questions.

title: Teach yesterday, today, and tomorrow
body: time words are abstract and they are learned from hearing them used about real events. yesterday we went to the park. tomorrow we will see grandma. use a calendar on the wall and point at the day. a child who understands yesterday and tomorrow at three is on track.

title: Name feelings out loud, including your own
body: a child who has words for a feeling has something to do with it other than hit. i am frustrated because the traffic is slow. you are disappointed that the park is closed. name it, do not fix it. a feelings chart on the wall helps. this is the foundation for the conversations at four and five.

title: Sentences of three or more words
body: most three-year-olds speak in sentences of three or more words and can be understood by strangers most of the time. a child who is not understood at three is worth raising at the visit.

title: An hour a day, and not alone
body: the recommendation for two to five is no more than an hour a day of high-quality content, watched with an adult. a screen alone in a room is the thing to avoid.

title: Month 34
body: preschool readiness is the question of the month, and it is about self-care more than letters. your child speaks in sentences, can pedal a tricycle, and can put on some clothes. they can follow a three-step instruction and are starting to play with other children rather than beside them. if you are pregnant again, the last weeks are a logistics problem. line up who takes the older child, and for how long. thirty-four months is when the child starts to be able to do things for themselves. the list is longer than you think, and it is the list preschool cares about.

title: Teach the self-care preschool expects
body: a preschool teacher can help a child who can do some of it themselves, and cannot help twenty who cannot. using the toilet alone, washing hands, opening a lunchbox, putting on shoes, and blowing a nose. practise at home, slowly, with no audience. a child who can do these at three settles faster on the first day.

title: Cut, draw, and build every day
body: fine motor skills are built by using the hands, and they are what writing is made of. blunt scissors and paper strips. chunky crayons and big paper. blocks and playdough. ten minutes a day is enough. do not correct the grip yet, and do not turn it into a lesson.

title: Practise the drop-off before the first day
body: a short, practised goodbye is easier than a first one on a morning when everyone is already late. visit the preschool together before the first day. meet the teacher. practise the goodbye at home: the same words, a hug, and out the door. on the day, keep it short and do not come back for one more hug.

title: Letters are a four-year-old skill
body: recognising the first letter of their name at three is on track. knowing the alphabet is not expected until four or five. reading to them is the thing that matters now.

title: Quiet time replaces the nap
body: a child who has dropped the nap still needs an hour of quiet time in the afternoon. a book and a bed, not a screen.

title: Month 35
body: one month left in this guide. the three-year visit is next month. your child speaks in sentences, can jump, pedal, and climb stairs alternating feet. they can follow a three-step instruction and are starting to understand that other people have feelings too. if you are pregnant again, the birth is close. the older child needs a plan and a person, not a surprise. thirty-five months is when the child starts to notice that you have feelings. it is a real change, and it is the beginning of empathy.

title: Book the three-year visit
body: this is the last visit in this guide, and it is the one where preschool readiness and language get checked. the three-year visit usually has no vaccines if the eighteen-month set is complete. the doctor will check language, movement, teeth, and growth, and will ask about preschool and toilet learning. bring the questions.

title: Point out how other people feel
body: empathy is taught by naming it, and a three-year-old can learn to notice it. she is crying because she fell. he is happy because it is his birthday. ask what the child thinks the other person feels, and do not correct the answer. this is the foundation for the social skills at four.

title: Let them do the whole thing, once a day
body: a child who can do one thing from start to finish has a reason to try the next one. pick one thing a day and let the child do all of it: pour the water, put on the shoes, feed the dog. it will be slow and it will be wrong. do not fix it in front of them. fix it later.

title: Eleven to thirteen hours, and maybe a nap
body: a three-year-old usually sleeps eleven to thirteen hours a day. some still nap, some do not. quiet time in the afternoon is the bridge for the ones who do not.

title: A dental check every six months
body: twenty baby teeth, and a check every six months. the first permanent tooth is years away, but the habit is not.

title: Month 36
body: three years. this is the last month in this guide, and the first month of the rest of it. your child speaks in sentences, can jump, pedal, climb, and draw a circle. they can follow a three-step instruction, name a friend, and are starting to understand that other people have feelings. three years of carrying a child is three years of a body doing more than it did before. if something hurts, it is worth a physio visit. three years is the end of this guide and it is not the end of the work. you know more than you did, and the next stage is a different guide rather than a harder one.

title: Go to the three-year visit
body: this is the last visit in this guide, and it is the one where preschool readiness and language get checked. the three-year visit usually has no vaccines if the eighteen-month set is complete. the doctor will check language, movement, teeth, and growth, and will ask about preschool and toilet learning. ask what the next visit is, which is at four.

title: Look back at where you started
body: three years is a long time, and the distance is easier to see when you look at it on purpose. open the history and read the first week. the things that felt impossible then are the things you do without thinking now. that is not luck, and it is worth noticing before the next stage starts.

title: Know what comes next
body: the guide ends at three, and the things that matter after three are different rather than harder. preschool, friendships, letters, and the first questions about the world. the pediatrician moves to yearly visits. the dental check stays at six months. the safety rules change from gates to street and water.

title: A thousand words, and sentences of three or more
body: most three-year-olds have around a thousand words and speak in sentences of three or more. a child who is not understood by strangers at three is worth raising at the visit.

title: You are allowed to be tired
body: three years of broken sleep, carrying, and worrying is a long time. if you have not had a check-up of your own since the birth, this is a good month for one.
